descripcion_es: Natural word combinations: make a decision, make a mistake, pay attention…
resumen: Collocations are combinations of words that a native speaker uses naturally (make a decision, heavy traffic). Translating them word for word from Spanish produces very typical mistakes.

explicacion.texto: There is no logical rule: you have to learn them as chunks. The trickiest verbs are make, do, take, have, pay and give, and the intensifying adjectives (heavy, strong, high, deep).

filas: We need to make a decision today.
do something wrong (es: cometer un error)
move forward, improve (es: hacer progresos, avanzar)
She made an effort to be polite.
study a subject in depth / trade with someone (es: investigar / hacer negocios)
We do business with Chinese firms.
try as hard as you can / cause damage (es: hacer lo posible / hacer daño)
Too much sun can do harm.
The board took the decision in May.
do something dangerous / act to deal with something (es: correr un riesgo / tomar medidas)
The government must take steps to cut emissions.
participate in / happen, be held (es: participar en / tener lugar)
The summit will take place in Seville.
We must take inflation into account.
The law will have an impact on rents.
listen or watch carefully / visit (es: prestar atención / hacer una visita)
give a speech / give a presentation
speak formally to an audience (es: pronunciar un discurso / hacer una presentación)
She gave a speech at the conference.
bring up an issue / make people aware (es: plantear una cuestión / concienciar)
The campaign aims to raise awareness.
finish on time / supply what is needed (es: cumplir un plazo / satisfacer la demanda)
agree after discussion (es: llegar a un acuerdo)
a lot of traffic / a lot of rain (es: tráfico denso / lluvia intensa)
coffee with a lot of flavour / powerful wind (es: café cargado / viento fuerte)
expensive / advanced or large (es: precio alto / nivel alto)
We are deeply concerned about the situation.
very improbable / strongly advised (es: muy improbable / muy recomendable)
It is highly unlikely to happen.
a key role / a major problem
a very important role / a serious problem (es: un papel clave / un problema grave)
Tourism plays a key role in Spain.
used or known by many people (es: muy extendido / muy conocido)
English is widely used in science.

ejemplos.frase: It took them weeks to reach an agreement.
ejemplos.traduccion: Tardaron semanas en llegar a un acuerdo.

ejemplos.frase: Please pay attention to the safety instructions.
ejemplos.traduccion: Presten atención a las instrucciones de seguridad, por favor.

ejemplos.frase: We got stuck in heavy traffic on the way to the airport.
ejemplos.traduccion: Nos quedamos atascados en un tráfico denso camino del aeropuerto.

ejemplos.frase: Tourism plays a key role in the Canary Islands.
ejemplos.traduccion: El turismo desempeña un papel clave en Canarias.

ejemplos.frase: The charity is trying to raise awareness of mental health.
ejemplos.traduccion: La organización benéfica intenta concienciar sobre la salud mental.

ejemplos.frase: It is highly unlikely that the match will be cancelled.
ejemplos.traduccion: Es muy improbable que se suspenda el partido.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: I did a mistake in the exam.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: I made a mistake in the exam.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: We must take into account the inflation.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: We must take inflation into account.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: With a short object, it goes between “take” and “into account”; also, no article.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: The meeting will have place on Monday.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: The meeting will take place on Monday.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: There was strong traffic this morning.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: There was heavy traffic this morning.

ejercicios.frase: Don't worry, everybody ___ mistakes when they start.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the collocation make a mistake from the first table: to do something wrong. The clue is the noun mistakes after the gap, which always goes with make. The subject everybody is singular, so the verb takes -s: makes. The classic Spanish speaker's error is do a mistake, which this card lists among its typical mistakes.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Make a mistake” = do something wrong (es: cometer un error).
ejercicios.traduccion: No te preocupes, todo el mundo comete errores cuando empieza.

por_opcion.makes: Correct: make a mistake is the fixed collocation for doing something wrong.
por_opcion.does: Do a mistake is the most common calque by Spanish speakers and is not correct; do goes with business, research, harm.
por_opcion.takes: Take does not combine with mistake; it goes with steps, risks, decisions (British).
por_opcion.has: Have a mistake is not said; at most, “there is a mistake” to say that something contains an error.

ejercicios.frase: The Olympic Games will ___ place in Brisbane in 2032.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is take place, to happen or be held, from the first table. The clue is the noun place right after the gap and the fact that we are talking about an event with a place and a date. Spanish “tener lugar” pushes you to say have place, but the English collocation uses take. Will + infinitive marks the future.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Take place” = happen, be held (es: tener lugar).
ejercicios.traduccion: Los Juegos Olímpicos se celebrarán en Brisbane en 2032.

por_opcion.take: Correct: take place means to happen, to be held.
por_opcion.have: Have place is a calque of Spanish “tener lugar” and does not exist in English.
por_opcion.make: Make place is not a collocation; at most, make room would mean “to make space”.
por_opcion.give: Give place does not have this meaning; give way means to yield (e.g. to traffic).

ejercicios.frase: Students should ___ attention to the instructions.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is pay attention, from the first table. The clue is the noun attention after the gap and the preposition to, which introduces what you are attending to. The English verb is pay, not lend or give: you “pay” attention (Spanish says “prestar atención”). After should comes the infinitive without to.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Pay attention” = listen or watch carefully (es: prestar atención).
ejercicios.traduccion: Los estudiantes deberían prestar atención a las instrucciones.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Put attention is a calque of Spanish “poner atención”; the correct collocation is pay attention.
Lend means to give something temporarily (money, objects), but with attention we use pay.
Make attention does not exist; the collocation is pay attention.

ejercicios.frase: There was very strong rain during the night.
respuestas: There was very heavy rain during the night.
There was heavy rain during the night.
ejercicios.explicacion: The second table and the card's typical mistakes say it: intense rain is heavy rain, just as dense traffic is heavy traffic. The clue is the noun rain, which does not combine with strong. Strong is used for wind or coffee. The sentence may or may not keep the intensifier very.
ejercicios.traduccion: Hubo una lluvia muy intensa durante la noche.

errores_previstos.respuesta: There was very strong rain during the night.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This leaves the sentence uncorrected: rain goes with heavy, not with strong.

errores_previstos.respuesta: There was very powerful rain during the night.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Powerful does not combine with rain; the collocation is heavy rain.

errores_previstos.respuesta: There was very big rain during the night.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Big does not combine with rain; the collocation is heavy rain.

ejercicios.frase: After long negotiations, the unions ___ an agreement with the employers.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is reach an agreement, from the first table. The clue is the direct object an agreement: reach is transitive and takes it directly, without a preposition. Spanish “llegar a” pushes you towards arrived, which would need at and is not used with agreements. The past reached fits the account of a negotiation that is already over.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Reach an agreement” = agree after discussion (es: llegar a un acuerdo).
ejercicios.traduccion: Tras largas negociaciones, los sindicatos llegaron a un acuerdo con los empresarios.

por_opcion.reached: Correct: reach an agreement is the fixed collocation and takes no preposition.
por_opcion.arrived: Arrive means to get to a place and would need at or in; with agreement it is a calque of Spanish.
por_opcion.did: Do an agreement does not exist; agreements are reached (reach) or signed (sign).
por_opcion.came: Come to an agreement exists, but it needs to; “came an agreement” is not grammatical.

glosario.definicion_l: being of or having to do with the northern United States and those loyal to the Union during the American Civil War · the United States (especially the northern states during the American Civil War)
a person or firm that employs workers

ejercicios.frase: We worked all weekend to ___ the deadline.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is meet a deadline, to finish something on time, from the first table. The clue is the noun deadline after the gap and the context of working all weekend. The verb meet, which usually means “get to know” or “get together”, here means to fulfil or satisfy, as in meet demand. After to comes the infinitive.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Meet a deadline” = finish on time (es: cumplir un plazo).
ejercicios.traduccion: Trabajamos todo el fin de semana para cumplir el plazo.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Fulfil means to carry out (a promise, a requirement), but with deadline the natural collocation is meet.
Comply means to obey a rule and needs with; it does not combine with deadline.
Arrive is not transitive and is not used with deadlines.

glosario.definicion_l: the point in time at which something must be completed

ejercicios.frase: My uncle does a lot of business in Mexico and did a big effort to learn the local customs.
respuestas: My uncle does a lot of business in Mexico and made a big effort to learn the local customs.
ejercicios.explicacion: The sentence combines two collocations from the first table: do business, which is correct, and make an effort, which is wrongly written as did a big effort. The clue is the noun effort, which always goes with make. You only need to change did to made and leave does a lot of business as it is. It is a good example of how Spanish “hacer” is split between make and do with no clear logic.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: We say “make an effort”; “do business” is correct.
ejercicios.traduccion: Mi tío hace muchos negocios en México y se esforzó mucho por aprender las costumbres locales.

errores_previstos.respuesta: My uncle does a lot of business in Mexico and did a big effort to learn the local customs.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This leaves the sentence uncorrected: effort goes with make, not with do.

errores_previstos.respuesta: My uncle makes a lot of business in Mexico and made a big effort to learn the local customs.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Effort has been corrected, but business has been spoilt: the correct collocation is do business.

errores_previstos.respuesta: My uncle does a lot of business in Mexico and took a big effort to learn the local customs.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Take an effort is not the collocation; we say make an effort.

ejercicios.frase: The minister ___ a speech at the opening ceremony.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is give a speech, from the first table. The clue is the noun a speech as the direct object. Make a speech also exists, as the exercise explanation notes, but it is not among the options. Say and tell do not form a collocation with speech: say goes with specific words and tell with people or stories.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Give a speech” = speak formally to an audience (es: pronunciar un discurso); also “make a speech”.
ejercicios.traduccion: El ministro pronunció un discurso en la ceremonia de inauguración.

por_opcion.gave: Correct: give a speech means to deliver a speech.
por_opcion.said: Say introduces what is said (said that…, said a few words), but does not combine with speech.
por_opcion.told: Tell needs a person or goes with story, joke, truth; “told a speech” is not said.
por_opcion.made up: Make up means to invent; “made up a speech” would mean inventing a speech, not delivering it.

ejercicios.frase: This restaurant is ___ recommended by local food critics.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is highly recommended, from the second table. The clue is the participle recommended: with it, and with unlikely or successful, the usual intensifier is highly, not very or high. Highly is the adverb of high, but here it does not refer to height but to degree. It is a very common collocation in reviews and formal texts.
ejercicios.traduccion: Este restaurante está muy recomendado por los críticos gastronómicos locales.

errores_previstos.explicacion: High is an adjective; to modify a participle you need the adverb highly.
Much recommended sounds old-fashioned and forced; the natural collocation is highly recommended.

ejercicios.frase: The new law will ___ a big impact on small farmers.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is have an impact on, to affect, from the first table. The clue is the noun impact followed by the preposition on. Here Spanish “tener” does match have; the risk is being led by “causar” or “hacer” un impacto. After will comes the infinitive have.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Have an impact on” = affect (es: repercutir en).
ejercicios.traduccion: La nueva ley tendrá un gran impacto en los pequeños agricultores.

por_opcion.have: Correct: have an impact on is the fixed collocation.
por_opcion.do: Do an impact is not said; do goes with harm, business, research.
por_opcion.give: Give an impact is not natural in English.
por_opcion.take: Take an impact does not exist with this meaning.

glosario.definicion_l: United States civil rights leader who in 1942 founded the Congress of Racial Equality (born in 1920) · an expert on cooking whose cookbook has undergone many editions (1857-1915)

ejercicios.frase: The campaign aims to ___ awareness of plastic pollution.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is raise awareness, to make people aware, from the first table. The clue is the noun awareness (knowledge, consciousness) followed by of. Raise means to lift, to increase, and also combines with a question (bring up an issue) or funds (collect money). After aims to comes the infinitive.
ejercicios.traduccion: La campaña pretende concienciar sobre la contaminación por plásticos.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Make awareness is a calque of Spanish “hacer conciencia” and does not exist; we say raise awareness.
Rise is intransitive (go up) and takes no object; the transitive verb is raise.
Do awareness does not exist; the collocation is raise awareness.

ejercicios.frase: I always drink very hard coffee in the morning.
respuestas: I always drink very strong coffee in the morning.
I always drink strong coffee in the morning.
ejercicios.explicacion: The second table includes strong coffee (es: café cargado). The clue is the noun coffee: in English coffee is strong or weak, never hard. Hard means firm or difficult and does not have the sense of concentrated. The intensifier very may stay or go.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Coffee with a lot of flavour is “strong coffee”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Siempre tomo un café muy cargado por la mañana.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I always drink very hard coffee in the morning.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This leaves the sentence uncorrected: concentrated coffee is strong, not hard.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I always drink very heavy coffee in the morning.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Heavy goes with rain or traffic, not with coffee.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I always drink very charged coffee in the morning.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Charged is a calque of Spanish “cargado” and is not used with drinks.

ejercicios.frase: The government must ___ urgent steps to reduce emissions.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is take steps, to act to deal with something, from the first table. The clue is the noun steps (measures). Here Spanish “tomar” matches take, but many people hesitate between make and do. We also say take measures or take action, always with take. After must comes the infinitive.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Take steps” = act to deal with something (es: tomar medidas).
ejercicios.traduccion: El Gobierno debe tomar medidas urgentes para reducir las emisiones.

por_opcion.take: Correct: take steps means to take measures.
por_opcion.make: Make steps is not the collocation; make goes with decision, progress, effort.
por_opcion.do: Do steps does not exist with this meaning.
por_opcion.give: Give steps is not natural in English.

glosario.definicion_l: the act of emitting; causing to flow forth · a substance that is emitted or released

ejercicios.frase: The fans were ___ disappointed by the result.
ejercicios.explicacion: The second table includes bitterly disappointed, extremely or bitterly let down; deeply disappointed is just as natural and profoundly disappointed, a bit more formal, is also correct, so all three are accepted. The clue is the adjective disappointed and the instruction, which asks for “deeply” (es: profundamente). They are adverbs, not adjectives: they end in -ly because they modify another adjective.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Bitterly / deeply / profoundly disappointed” = extremely disappointed (es: profundamente decepcionado).
ejercicios.traduccion: Los aficionados quedaron profundamente decepcionados con el resultado.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Deep is an adjective; to intensify the adjective disappointed you need the adverb deeply.
Very much does not go before an adjective like disappointed; for “deeply” we use bitterly or deeply.
Strongly goes with opinion verbs (strongly agree, strongly recommend), not with disappointed.

glosario.definicion_l: a device for creating a current of air by movement of a surface or surfaces · an enthusiastic devotee of sports

respuestas: Tourism plays a key role in Spain
In Spain tourism plays a key role
Tourism in Spain plays a key role
ejercicios.explicacion: This is play a key role, from the second table. The verb is play, just as an actor plays a part in a play; key goes before role because adjectives come before the noun. The phrase in Spain can go at the end, at the beginning or right after tourism (Tourism in Spain plays a key role, “tourism in Spain”), so all three orders are accepted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Play a key role” = have a very important function (es: desempeñar un papel clave).
ejercicios.traduccion: El turismo desempeña un papel clave en España.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Tourism plays a role key in Spain
errores_previstos.explicacion: The adjective key goes before the noun: a key role.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Tourism in Spain plays a role key
errores_previstos.explicacion: This puts key after role, as in Spanish; in English the adjective goes before: a key role.

descripcion_larga_es: Collocations are combinations of words that native speakers naturally use together, such as make a decision, heavy traffic or pay attention. They do not follow a logic you can work out, so you have to learn them as chunks. They are the difference between correct English and English that sounds translated; Spanish speakers are tripped up by the verbs make, do, take and have and by intensifying adjectives.

contexto.que_es: A collocation is a usual combination of words: a verb with its noun (make a mistake, take steps), an adjective with its noun (heavy rain, strong coffee) or an adverb with its adjective (highly recommended, bitterly disappointed). Other combinations would be grammatically possible, but a native speaker would not use them.
contexto.por_que_importa: A wrong collocation rarely prevents understanding, but it sounds strange and gives away the literal translation, which costs a lot in a B2-level exam or higher, where range and naturalness of vocabulary are assessed. In economic and administrative texts they are everywhere: reach an agreement, meet a deadline, take steps, have an impact on.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: In any register, but above all when writing reports or formal emails, or giving oral presentations. The warning sign is a very frequent noun (decision, mistake, effort, attention, rain, traffic) that requires a specific verb or adjective. Spanish speakers tend to translate “hacer”, “tomar” or “fuerte” word for word, and that is where they go wrong.
